lessons.title: ೂ (ū) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ೂ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ೂ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಅ — which way did the pen travel first?
One character this time — a mark rather than a letter, and one that has quietly been changing the meaning of whole sentences.

It is a vowel sign, not a letter: it never stands alone. Hang it on a consonant and the built-in a becomes a long ū. You have had the full letter ಊ for the start of a word; this is the same sound, worn inside one.
You already say these, and every one of them has ೂ (ū) somewhere inside it:
ನಾನೂ nānū — I too, from the joining lesson.
ಹೂವು hūvu — a flower.
ಮೂಗು mūgu — the nose.
ಕೂದಲು kūdalu — hair.
Put your pen on ೂ (ū) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.text: Which character is this — ೂ? What sound does it carry? (ū.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
Before the new one: which sign did you trace last, and what does gottilla mean?
ಗೊತ್ತಾ (gottā) — "do you know?"
It is ಗೊತ್ತು with its ending swapped for a long -ಆ (-ā), and that ending is the whole question. Nothing else moved: no word order changed, nothing was added in front.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one ending turns any statement into a question

segments.text: Put -ಆ on the end of a statement and the statement becomes a yes-or-no question. That is the entire machinery.
You have been saying it since the third chapter without being told, inside ನೀವು ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ (nīvu hēgiddīrā) — the -ā on the end is this one.
Every sentence you own can now be asked. ಚಹಾ ಇದೆ becomes ಚಹಾ ಇದೆಯಾ ("is there tea?"); ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೊತ್ತು becomes ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೊತ್ತಾ (gottā). And the answer is the echo you learned first: ಹೌದು, or ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ.
Every statement in this book, asked.

segments.text: What turns a Kannada statement into a yes-or-no question? (The ending -ಆ.) Ask somebody whether they know.

lessons.title: ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) — isn't it?
lessons.gloss: isn't it? — the tag on the end

segments.text: Before the new one: which ending makes a question, and what does gottā ask?
ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) — "isn't it?", "right?"

Two things you already have, pushed together. ಅಲ್ಲ ("is not") takes the question ending -ಆ and becomes ಅಲ್ಲವಾ (allavā) — "is it not?". In ordinary speech that flattens to ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā), and it is the flattened one you will hear.
ಇದು ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ ಪುಸ್ತಕ, ಅಲ್ವಾ? (idu oḷḷeya pustaka, alvā?) — "this is a good book, isn't it?"
Register, plainly: ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) is spoken Kannada. Written Kannada says ಅಲ್ಲವೇ. This book teaches the everyday spoken variety throughout, so ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) is what you get here.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: asking for agreement, not information

segments.text: Somebody who says ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) usually knows the answer already; they are inviting you to agree, and they expect ಹೌದು.
That makes it the cheapest politeness move in the language. A flat statement can land as a correction; the same statement with ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) on the end hands the other person a share of it.
A question you can ask about anything, and a tag that softens it.

segments.instruction: alla, then allavā, then alvā
idu oḷḷeya pustaka, alvā?
say something true about this room and add alvā
segments.source: [YOU SAY: say something true about this room and add *alvā*]

segments.instruction: say gottā, then answer it
say hālū illa, nīrū illa once more
segments.source: [YOU RECALL: say *hālū illa, nīrū illa* once more]

segments.source: [YOU RECALL: from much earlier — say *candra*, *kēḷu*, *nōḍu*, *koḍu*, and say what each one means]

segments.text: What does ಅಲ್ವಾ (alvā) ask for? (Agreement.) Which two pieces is it made of? (alla and the question ending -ಆ.)
Before the new one: what does alvā invite the other person to do?
ಯಾಕೆ (yāke) — "why?"
The question words came in a set: ಯಾರು (yāru, "who"), ಎಲ್ಲಿ (elli, "where"), ಏನು (ēnu, "what"). ಯಾಕೆ (yāke) is the one the set was missing, and it is the one a short conversation runs out of first.
ಯಾಕೆ (yāke)? on its own is a whole turn. Somebody says they are not coming; you say ಯಾಕೆ (yāke), and you have asked the only question that matters.

You will also meet ಏಕೆ (ēke) for the same word. It is the careful, written form; ಯಾಕೆ (yāke) is what gets said. Keep the two side by side — the word for "because" is built on the written one, and it is not far off.
Four question words now, and the one that opens a reason. Asking why is half of a conversation; the other half is the answer, and that is next.

yāru, elli, yāke — three questions in a row

lessons.title: ಲ (la) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ಲ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಲ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ೂ (ū) — what does it do to the consonant it sits on?
One character this time — and it is the one standing in the middle of both of Kannada's negatives.
ಲ — la.

It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not l, it is la. Kannada has a second l as well — the thicker ಳ you already trace — and the two are different letters for different sounds, not a matter of handwriting.
You already say these, and every one of them has ಲ (la) somewhere inside it:
ಅಲ್ಲ alla — is not (that).
ಇಲ್ಲ illa — there is not.
ಹಲ್ಲು hallu — a tooth.
ಕಾಲು kālu — a leg.
Put your pen on ಲ and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
